cases.name: devnet_like
cases.why: A submission of the shape the devnet batcher posts. Every cursor field differs from every other, so a reader that transposed two of them cannot land on this answer.

cases.name: empty_cert
cases.why: A submission whose certificate is zero bytes. The payload is a length word and nothing else, so the certifierSig offset is the smallest it ever is and an encoder that padded an empty payload to a whole word would be caught here.

cases.name: empty_commitment
cases.why: A submission whose eigenda_commitment is zero bytes. The wire admits it -- the contract refuses it later, as COMMITMENT_MISMATCH -- and its payload is a bare length word, so an encoder that padded an empty payload to a whole word is caught here.

cases.name: commitment_length_not_a_whole_number_of_words
cases.why: A 33-byte eigenda_commitment, so its tail carries 31 zero bytes of padding before the certifier_sig length word. The canonical encoding for any length the wire carries, not only EIGENDA_CODEC's 64.

cases.name: cert_length_not_a_whole_number_of_words
cases.why: A 33-byte certificate: one word plus one byte, so abi.encode pads the tail with 31 zero bytes. Those zeros are not slack -- a body carrying anything else there is a different byte string for the same fields, which is exactly what the canonicality rule refuses.

cases.name: max_fields
cases.why: Every numeric field at the maximum its declared width holds, and the bitmap with every bit set. A reader that truncated height to 32 bits, or read index as a uint64, agrees with the canonical encoding on every other case and not on this one.

cases.name: long_cert
cases.why: A 200-byte certificate. The certifierSig offset is seven words past the head here, so the encoding where that offset was written second instead of last -- one of the three wire bugs this vector exists for -- produces a body nothing can read back.

cases.name: trailing_byte
cases.why: The canonical body with one byte after the last field. Every offset still points where it did and every field reads back, so a reader that stopped at the last field it needed accepts two different byte strings for one submission -- and op-batcher puts exactly one of them on L1.

cases.name: trailing_word
cases.why: A whole zero word appended. The same rule as the trailing byte, in the shape a padding mistake produces rather than a truncation one: zeros look like slack and are not.

cases.name: wrap_offset_not_the_minimal_32
cases.why: The offset abi.encode wraps a single struct argument in, moved from 32 to 64 with a zero word inserted so it still points at the tuple. abi.decode follows it and every field reads back; the encoding is simply not the one this submission has. A reader without the re-encode accepts unboundedly many bodies per submission.

cases.name: cert_offset_non_minimal
cases.why: The eigendaCert offset pushed one word past where the encoder writes it, with a zero word inserted so the payload is still there and both offsets still resolve. This is the non-minimal-offset family that Go's ABI decoder tolerates by design.

cases.name: swapped_offsets
cases.why: The eigendaCert and certifierSig offsets exchanged. Both still resolve, so a reader that followed offsets and stopped there reads the signature as the certificate and the certificate as the signature. The contract reports TeeSigLengthInvalid rather than the encoding, and that is the rule order working rather than a surprise: certifierSig now resolves to the 33-byte certificate, so the length check fires before the re-encode equality is ever reached. The verdict here was run, not predicted -- which is the reason this file records what _decode did instead of what a rule says it should.

cases.name: body_that_is_not_an_encoding_at_all
cases.why: Four bytes behind a correct prefix. The prefix is not evidence about the body, and a reader that admitted on the strength of two bytes would settle on nothing.

cases.name: empty_body
cases.why: The prefix and nothing after it. Distinct from calldata shorter than the prefix: here the transaction protocol is satisfied and the payload is absent.

cases.name: body_truncated_mid_head
cases.why: The canonical body cut inside the head, so the certifierSig offset word is not there to read. A decoder that read past the buffer, or treated a missing word as zero, is caught here.

cases.name: certifier_sig_64_bytes
cases.why: A canonical body whose signature is one byte short. It re-encodes to itself exactly, so the canonicality rule admits it and only TEE_SIG_BYTES catches it -- which is why the contract checks the length first and why only the contract column rejects here. op-node and the Rust wrapper accept it, correctly: a reader that refused it would refuse bytes on the strength of a rule that is not its own.

cases.name: certifier_sig_66_bytes
cases.why: One byte long, the other side of the same rule. It also re-encodes to itself, so the length is again the only thing that can refuse it.

cases.name: prefix_generic_commitment_type
cases.why: 0x01 0x01: the legacy GenericCommitmentType the alt-DA provider this inbox replaces posts. This is the case the compatibility branch exists for -- the legacy batcher runs eth_estimateGas against this address until cutover -- and the body behind it is a perfectly canonical certified commitment, so nothing but the second byte distinguishes it.

cases.name: prefix_legacy_eigenda_proxy
cases.why: 0x01 0x01 0x00: the three-byte opening of the 546 real op-batcher captures in crosstest/fixtures/commitment_decode.json, where the third byte is eigenda-proxy's DA-layer id. Recorded here from the real shape rather than invented, because the prefix rule's whole job is to tell this apart from a certified submission.

cases.name: prefix_foreign_derivation_version
cases.why: 0x00 0x80: the certified commitment type under a derivation version this inbox does not know. Checking only the second byte would admit it.

cases.name: prefix_foreign_commitment_type
cases.why: 0x01 0xff: upstream's reference server puts 0xff in this position. Checking only the first byte would admit it.

cases.name: prefix_retired_certified_type
cases.why: 0x01 0x02: the certified commitment type before spec c8a22ee moved it to 0x80, the opening the shadow inbox's Sepolia submissions in vectors/sepolia_certified_txs.json carry. It is a foreign type now like any other, so a reader that kept 0x02 as an alias would admit calldata the inbox treats as a legacy-format call.

cases.name: no_prefix_at_all
cases.why: The encoded commitment posted bare -- what a contract that believed the body starts at offset zero would be built for. This is the first of the three wire bugs, as calldata.

cases.name: one_prefix_byte_dropped
cases.why: 0x01 followed by the body: the off-by-one. The derivation version still matches, so a reader checking one byte accepts it and then decodes from an offset one byte out.

cases.name: calldata_shorter_than_the_prefix
cases.why: A single byte. Both readers have to reach the length check before the byte comparison, or they index past the end of calldata.

cases.name: empty_calldata
cases.why: No calldata at all.

note: Solidity writes this file and Rust and Go read it. Each case states facts about the bytes -- whether the prefix is the certified pair, whether the body is the canonical encoding of its own fields, and what BatchInbox._decode did -- rather than one merged verdict, because the three readers deliberately enforce different rules. The prefix is a transaction-protocol rule that op-node and the contract read and the Rust wrapper never sees; the 65-byte certifierSig length is a contract rule that neither of the other two has an opinion about; canonicality is shared by all three. Each consumer maps these facts to its own rules in one line. eigendaCert is arbitrary bytes because none of the three readers decodes the certificate. Version 2 is the spec 513524d wire: BatchCommitment(bytes eigenda_cert, bytes eigenda_commitment, Cursor prev_cursor, Cursor cursor, bytes certifier_sig), a fifteen-word tuple head. Version 3 is spec c8a22ee, which moves CERTIFIED_COMMITMENT_TYPE from 0x02 to 0x80, outside the OP Stack reserved range 0x00..0x7f, so BATCH_TX_PREFIX is 0x0180; every body is unchanged and only the second calldata byte moved.
server_key: block_certifier_server's store key is the CertifiedCommitmentType byte followed by the body: 0x80 ++ body_hex. SubmissionKey::of rebuilds exactly that from a decoded submission, which is the round trip crates/types' consumer asserts.
